newsitem.title: USA: Magnesium steels for growth in desulfurization.
newsitem.headline: Magnesium steels for growth in desulfurization.

text.p: The use of magnesium, especially recycled metal, to purify or desulfurize steel is set to grow over despite cheaper alternatives, Gerald Zebrowski, president and CEO of Rossborough Manufacturing Co said.

In 1996 the amount of magnesium used in desulfurizing steel in North America totaled 31,100 tonnes, up from 27,700 tonnes in the previous year. Recycled magnesium accounted for 4,700 tonnes of last year's total, Zebrowski estimated.
Desulfurization is the third largest user of magnesium after aluminum alloying and diecasting auto parts.
The International Magnesium Association, of which Zebrowski is vice-president, only publishes data on primary or virgin magnesium.
The IMA wants to publish data on recycled metal but secondary producers would have to be more forthcoming with information, Zebrowski told Metal Bulletin's Minor Metals Seminar here.
Rossborough buys magnesium to make products for desulfurizing steel.

Die cast auto parts is a big growth area for magnesium, and when scrapped, some 10 to 15 percent of the recycled metal will not be acceptable to diecasters but can be used in desulfurization, therefore tracking secondary magnesium trends was essential, Zebrowski said.

Greater availability of recycled metal will be crucial in plugging any supply gaps created by Russia and China's steel industries consuming more and more of domestically produced magnesium in desulfurizing when the light metal was previously exported to the West, Zebrowski said.

The use of magnesium in desulfurization is extremely price sensitive, and cheaper alternatives such as calcium carbide, soda ash and lime are used by some steelmakers when magnesium prices rise sharply, Zebrowski said.

Magnesium has nearly reached saturation in North America's desulfurization sector, but should remain at 30,000 to 35,000 tonnes a year. Western European steelmakers use greater amounts of calcium carbide but environmental concerns should create an opportunity for magnesium consumption to reach 20,000 to 25,000 tonnes a year.

Japan has a potential desulfurization market of 10,000 tonnes a year or greater while in China, after becoming the world's biggest steelmaker last year, the potential for magnesium consumption is enormous and should eventually equal or surpass the North American total, Zebrowski said.

Central and Eastern Europe should reach comparable levels as Western European demand. In Latin America, Brazil and Argentina have large steelmaking capacities and are now installing magnesium based desulfurizing equipment, with a potential to reach 6,000 to 8,000 tonnes a year.
Turning to pricing of magnesium, Zebrowski said a futures contract in magnesium would be of interest to desulfurizer makers and to the steel industry.

"From our standpoint it's our lifeblood to try and anticipate the price of magnesium," Zebrowski said. The steel industry wanted long-term contracts over one to seven years to buy magnesium but magnesium producers do not like to enter long- term sales contracts.
"We try to include some indexing but there is no perfect way to do it, so I suppose if there was a futures market it would be quite interesting for us," Zebrowski added.
